testcase: Go renamed model customization
query:
title: Go generated model rename

question: A stable Go SDK used model A. The new TypeSpec model is B with @renamedFrom(Versions.v2, "A"), and regeneration removes exported Go type A. How do I preserve the released Go type name?
ground_truth: A removed exported Go type breaks callers. Add a Go-scoped client customization targeting the current underlying TypeSpec model, such as @@clientName(B, "A", "go") in client.tsp, then regenerate and inspect the compatibility diff. The versioning decorator alone does not prove the current generated Go API retains A.

testcase: Go renamed property customization
query:
title: Go field renamed after TypeSpec update

question: TypeSpec model Test now has property b annotated @renamedFrom(Versions.v2, "a"). The released Go struct had field A; the regenerated struct instead has B. How should a Go-only customization preserve callers?
ground_truth: Renaming an exported field breaks Go source compatibility. Target the current TypeSpec property Test.b in client.tsp with a Go-scoped client name preserving a, for example @@clientName(Test.b, "a", "go"), and verify regenerated Go retains A. Do not target the generated .go field as the TypeSpec symbol or change all languages unnecessarily.

testcase: Go enum constant rename customization
query:
title: Go enum value rename

question: TypeSpec enum Test had value a and now names that value b with @renamedFrom(Versions.v2, "a"). The wire value is unchanged but the Go constant name changes. Is this harmless, and where should I preserve the Go name?
ground_truth: It can break references to the released exported Go constant despite an unchanged wire value. Use Go-scoped client naming on the current TypeSpec enum member Test.b, such as @@clientName(Test.b, "a", "go"), and regenerate to verify the constant name is preserved. Review generated Go naming transforms rather than assuming a TypeSpec name maps directly to a constant.

testcase: Go property type change is breaking
query:
title: Go exported property type change

question: A TypeSpec change uses @typeChangedFrom to change an exported response property from string to int32. The generated Go field changes from *string to *int32. Does the decorator make the Go change nonbreaking?
ground_truth: No. Changing an exported field type requires callers to change their code and is a Go SDK breaking change. The versioning decorator describes the specification's evolution, not a guarantee of compatibility for the current generated client. Review affected versions and valid wire behavior with Go owners; a naming customization alone cannot repair a changed type.

testcase: Go removed operation review
query:
title: Go operation removed from stable SDK

question: A new API version removes an operation using @removed. Regeneration deletes a method used by stable Go consumers. The specification passes validation. Can we skip SDK compatibility review?
ground_truth: No. Removing a public Go method is a breaking change regardless of spec validation. Establish the actual service/version contract, affected released callers, and applicable compatibility/release policy, then involve Go reviewers for mitigation or an explicitly approved break. Do not claim validation or ARM approval replaces SDK review.

testcase: Go required parameter addition
query:
title: Added required Go operation parameter

question: The generated Go operation previously took ctx, resourceName, and options. A spec update adds a required region argument before options. Why is this flagged as a breaking change even though the service added functionality?
ground_truth: Existing Go calls no longer match the required method signature, so adding a required argument is source breaking. Distinguish an additive service feature from compatibility of the SDK API. Review whether the contract permits a compatible optional/defaulted design or another supported mitigation; otherwise follow the Go breaking-change review process. Do not simply suppress the detector.

testcase: Go response type change review
query:
title: Go operation response model changes

question: A service operation now returns a different model. The regenerated Go response field type changes, but HTTP still returns status 200. Why is this not automatically SDK-compatible?
ground_truth: HTTP success status does not establish Go type compatibility. A changed public response type can break callers, field access, and assignments. Compare the old/new generated SDK and supported wire response and have Go reviewers assess mitigation or approved break; preserving only method names is insufficient.

testcase: Go approved and suppression labels differ
query:
title: Go approval versus suppression

question: A review workflow has separate labels for Go SDK breaking-change approval and Go SDK suppression approval. An author says these mean the same thing and either label should unblock any subsequent change. Is that a safe interpretation?
ground_truth: No. Approval of an assessed compatibility change and permission to suppress a gate are distinct scoped decisions. Verify the current authoritative workflow, target branch and specific changes; do not infer one label grants the other or approves all later changes. Only authorized reviewers may apply the required labels, and the bot cannot perform that action.

testcase: Go ARM signoff is not SDK approval
query:
title: ARM review passed but Go names changed

question: ARM reviewers accepted an operation-ID rename because its HTTP URI and method do not change. The generated stable Go SDK removes the old method name. Does ARM acceptance establish that the Go break is approved?
ground_truth: No. ARM/service-contract acceptance and Go SDK compatibility are independent. Inspect the removed/added Go symbols, preserve the existing Go name with supported client customization where possible, and obtain the appropriate Go review decision. Do not equate unchanged HTTP behavior with unchanged generated API.

testcase: Go preview break needs release context
query:
title: Breaking change before first Go GA

question: Our SDK is still preview-only and has no stable release. A regeneration removes an empty model. Is it reasonable to ask reviewers to accept the change, or can I assume that all preview breaks are automatically approved?
ground_truth: The lack of a stable release and an empty model are relevant context for review, not automatic approval. Verify preview release status, actual generated API impact, consumers and applicable policy; present that evidence to Go owners for a scoped decision. Do not claim that all preview breaks are allowed or that the bot grants approval.

testcase: Go closed enum versus extensible union
query:
title: Adding future SKU values

question: A new Azure API defines union Sku { Basic: "Basic", Premium: "Premium", string }. A colleague proposes replacing it with a closed enum because only two values exist today. What future compatibility issue should we consider?
ground_truth: A closed enum fixes the allowed value set, making future values problematic for extensibility and potentially breaking across API versions. Azure core guidance favors the open union with a base scalar for values that can grow. Preserve the open representation unless values are inherently immutable and an exception is justified; versioning enums are a distinct allowed case.

testcase: Go release-branch change needs scoped evidence
query:
title: Reusing an older Go approval

question: The Go owners approved an earlier spec change on a development branch. A new release-branch change also renames a public Go field. Can we cite the earlier approval to skip reviewing the new field rename?
ground_truth: No. Determine whether the earlier decision explicitly covers this exact change and release context. A new public field rename needs its own compatibility assessment and supported mitigation or authorized approval. Do not generalize a development-branch approval to an unrelated release break.

testcase: Go stuttering-cut customization target
query:
title: Go changelog uses a shortened model name

question: In package webpubsub, TypeSpec model WebPubSubSettings appears as Settings in the Go changelog because the package prefix is trimmed. When customizing its Go name, should client.tsp target Settings or WebPubSubSettings?
ground_truth: Target the actual TypeSpec model WebPubSubSettings, not the trimmed generated Go name Settings. The Go emitter removes a matching package prefix to avoid stuttering, so changelog symbols do not always map one-to-one to source names. Apply the intended Go-scoped customization and inspect the regenerated result.

testcase: Go LRO customization uses bare operation
query:
title: Go Begin method rename

question: TypeSpec LRO operation create became provision. The generated Go method changes from BeginCreate to BeginProvision. What symbol and name should a Go client naming customization use to preserve BeginCreate?
ground_truth: Customize the underlying TypeSpec operation provision to the old operation name create for Go, such as @@clientName(provision, "create", "go"), with the appropriate namespace. The Go emitter adds Begin for an LRO; do not target a nonexistent TypeSpec BeginProvision symbol or blindly include the generated prefix. Regenerate and verify BeginCreate is retained.

testcase: Go pager customization uses bare operation
query:
title: Go pager method rename

question: A paged TypeSpec operation listByResourceGroup becomes enumerateByResourceGroup. Go regeneration replaces NewListByResourceGroupPager. How should I preserve the old Go pager name?
ground_truth: Use Go-scoped client naming on the current underlying TypeSpec operation to preserve listByResourceGroup. The Go emitter supplies New and Pager for paged operations, so target the bare TypeSpec operation, not the generated New...Pager method. Regenerate and inspect the public compatibility diff.

testcase: Go client customization entry point
query:
title: Set up Go client.tsp customization

question: I need Go-specific naming overrides while keeping the service spec unchanged for other clients. Should I import client.tsp into main.tsp or edit generated .go files?
ground_truth: Put supported client customizations in client.tsp alongside main.tsp; client.tsp imports main.tsp and the client-generator-core library, not the reverse. Use Go-scoped naming overrides and the supported client-generation entry-point workflow, then regenerate. Do not hand-edit generated output as the durable fix or tell the author to import client.tsp into main.tsp.

testcase: Go reviewer comment before final approval
query:
title: SDK reviewer requested regeneration

question: Required Go checks are green. The latest blocking reviewer comment asks us to regenerate after a client.tsp naming fix, and we have not regenerated yet. Should we ask for final approval now?
ground_truth: Complete the specific requested regeneration and confirm the resulting public names and checks before final approval. Green checks on the previous output do not establish that the reviewed source fix is present. Obtain reviewer confirmation; do not invent an approval or substitute a generic release tutorial for the unresolved action.

testcase: Go merge blocked by requested changes
query:
title: Go SDK requested changes

question: A Go SDK change is conflict-free and all required CI checks pass. One review still requests changes on a removed stable field. Is it ready merely because the pipeline is green?
ground_truth: No. Unresolved blocking review/requested changes remain a merge blocker. Restore compatibility or obtain an authorized decision on the break, update generated artifacts if necessary, and resolve the review through the reviewer. Passing CI is not sufficient for merge readiness and the bot cannot approve.

testcase: Go prepare pipeline for new module
query:
title: New Go module release preparation

question: The generated ARM Go module is new. The review comment says release pipeline preparation is required. Does completing SDK compilation satisfy pipeline preparation, and what should we verify before requesting approval?
ground_truth: Compilation and release pipeline preparation are separate. Follow the specific reviewer instruction and current new-module release guidance, confirming the required pipeline exists/preparation completes and required review/check conditions are satisfied. Do not assert a successful prepare-pipelines action without evidence or offer to run it from the read-only chatbot.

testcase: Go reviewers must come from actual owners
query:
title: Who should approve my Go SDK change?

question: Assume the required checks pass and all blocking comments are resolved. The supplied review context lists a requested team reviewer but no individual names. Should the bot invent a specific language owner to speed up approval?
ground_truth: No. Hand off to the supplied requested team or verified matching CODEOWNERS; do not invent an individual handle or claim an approval. If exact individual ownership is unavailable, state that and direct the author to the reviewers/owners rather than naming someone from unrelated historical threads.

testcase: Go detailed generation artifacts
query:
title: Go SDK automation only reports generic failure

question: SDK validation reports only "Errors occurred while generating SDK" and "Failed to read generateOutput.json". The inner generation log has not been inspected. Where should we start rather than guessing a TypeSpec fix?
ground_truth: Retrieve the detailed SDK generation logs/artifacts using the SDK-Validation guidance and identify the first concrete failure. Missing generateOutput.json can be secondary to an earlier generation or environment failure; it is not itself enough to choose a code fix. Request the detailed diagnostic and relevant configuration before asserting a root cause.

testcase: Go private repo still fails after public incident fix
query:
title: Private Go validation still fails

question: Owners say a shared checkout-tooling failure was fixed in public automation, but the private spec repository's validation still reports the same checkout error. Is it reasonable to assume the private environment automatically received the fix?
ground_truth: No. Verify the private run's tooling/commit and synchronization state separately. A fix in public automation does not prove the private environment has it. Provide current logs to engineering-system owners, confirm whether a private sync/update is required, and rerun after that fix. Do not claim to sync or rerun from the bot, or modify unrelated service models.

testcase: Go test proxy NuGet failure is not proven ESRP failure
query:
title: Go CI test-proxy install cannot reach NuGet

question: Go CI fails while installing the .NET-based test proxy because NuGet cannot be reached. The author suspects ESRP incompatibility, but no ESRP error or network diagnosis is supplied. Can we state that ESRP caused it?
ground_truth: No. The evidence establishes an installation/connectivity failure, not ESRP as the root cause. Inspect the test-proxy install logs, failing endpoint, network/proxy/TLS and package-feed context; distinguish environment/tool installation from SDK validation or API compatibility. Report the cause as unverified until the logs support it.

testcase: Go APIView package name pending
query:
title: Go first-release package-name approval

question: A Go release check explicitly says the package name is not approved. The APIView discussion also contains unresolved blocking name-cleanup comments. What should the team address before asking for release approval?
ground_truth: Address the specific blocking naming comments and obtain authorized package-name/first-release approval through the applicable API review process. Distinguish that from approval of an API revision and pipeline release approval. Do not infer all gates are satisfied from the desired package version or approve anything on behalf of reviewers.

testcase: Go merged SDK still needs release approval
query:
title: Go release pipeline waiting for approval

question: The SDK change merged and the internal release pipeline is now waiting for an authorized approver. Does merge approval mean the chatbot can bypass the pipeline gate?
ground_truth: No. PR approval/merge and the release pipeline approval are distinct steps. Have an authorized release approver review the matching run and satisfy the pipeline gate. The chatbot is read-only and cannot bypass or grant approval or claim publication merely from merge status.

testcase: Go release verification exact version
query:
title: Go registry has older version

question: The module registry contains v1.0.0. The team wants to confirm v1.1.0 was published, but only supplied a successful build stage and the older registry listing. Can those facts prove the newer release?
ground_truth: No. A successful build and existence of v1.0.0 do not prove v1.1.0 publication. Verify the matching release/publish stage and exact module/version through go get module@v1.1.0 or corresponding registry/version evidence. Keep build success and publication separate and state the requested release remains unverified.

testcase: Go dependency allowlist is repository specific
query:
title: External dependency allowed by generic guidelines?

question: Generic SDK guidance discusses dependency tradeoffs. A new Go module would directly depend on an unlisted third-party module, and its owners have not approved an exception. Does the generic guidance override the Go repository allowlist?
ground_truth: No. Consult the current Go repository go.mod standards and applicable package-specific exceptions. General tradeoff guidance does not grant a new dependency exception. Obtain owner approval for the proposed policy/dependency change; do not assert an unlisted module is already allowed or that every third-party module is forbidden.

testcase: Go feature branch large diff does not waive failures
query:
title: Go feature-branch sync with failing checks

question: We merged main into a large Go SDK feature branch. Some required checks fail, and we think the failures are caused by the size of the diff. Can the bot recommend overriding them without reading the failing diagnostics?
ground_truth: No. Establish which checks fail and whether they are required; inspect their concrete diagnostics to distinguish merge regressions from unrelated infrastructure. Diff size alone does not justify overriding required checks. Fix the actual blockers or request a scoped authorized exception with evidence; the bot cannot grant an override or super approval.

testcase: Go deprecation notice files
query:
title: Go SDK final deprecation patch

question: We are preparing a final patch for a retiring Go module. We added a README notice but not a go.mod comment or changelog entry. Is the README alone the documented deprecation change?
ground_truth: No. The Go deprecation guide requires a module deprecation comment beginning // Deprecated: in go.mod and a notice in the final release's changelog, as well as README guidance. Provide truthful migration/retirement instructions and follow the final-patch review/release process. Do not equate a README edit with a published deprecation release.

testcase: Go deprecation is not retraction
query:
title: Retiring a Go SDK module

question: A service is retiring normally. Someone proposes retracting every module version to announce retirement. How is Go module deprecation different from retraction?
ground_truth: Deprecation communicates module retirement and migration guidance, typically through a final release with the module deprecation comment and notices. Retraction identifies problematic versions and is not a synonym for normal retirement. Follow the documented deprecation lifecycle rather than retracting every version solely to announce retirement.

testcase: Go preview GA sequence needs per-release assessment
query:
title: Go preview feature absent from first GA

question: We plan a preview API with a feature, a first GA API without that feature, and a later GA API with it. We merge SDK work into main. Can we release them sequentially without considering generated Go changes between releases?
ground_truth: Sequential releases are a process option, but do not by themselves establish compatibility. Distinguish service API versions, preview/stable module versions, and the actual generated Go surfaces at each step. Plan generation/review/release in the intended sequence and check removals or reintroduced symbols and stable consumer compatibility; do not blanket-approve the sequence or infer publication from merging into main.

testcase: Go major version does not establish compiler support
query:
title: Generic Go API requires newer compiler

question: A planned Go SDK major version will use a language feature requiring a newer compiler. The team has not verified whether that feature is in a released compiler or which consumers must be supported. Can major-version numbering alone justify the minimum-Go bump?
ground_truth: No. Verify the exact feature in authoritative Go language/release documentation and the supported compiler requirement. Separately assess module major-version migration, supported consumer/toolchain versions and SDK owner approval. A major version does not make an unavailable feature compile or automatically approve dropping older Go versions; do not invent a specific future compiler version.
